newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries open lower on profit-taking.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries open lower on profit-taking.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries opened lower on Monday with profit-taking softening prices after Friday's rally.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond opened at 97-27/32, down 6/32 from Friday's close, and yielding 6.79 percent.

The 30-year bond yield ended at 6.78 percent on Friday, its lowest closing yield since February 28, after buying by foreign investors and domestic retail accounts, technical factors and short-covering spurred the market higher, erasing losses incurred after release of the May U.S. employment report.
Analysts said the dollar's weakness against the mark and yen was putting some pressure on Treasury prices.
"The market's come off lower because of the dollar weakness," said David Sloan, senior economist at I.D.E.A.
And Sloan said some profit-taking could be expected given the nature of Friday's rally.

"We did have a big, strong run-up on Friday that looked a bit suspicious given that the data in the May payroll report looked strong," he said. Sloan said Friday's rally was "mainly guided by foreign buying" after the French election raised fears that the European currencies are fragile.
Observing that there would be no new economic data to steer the market on Monday, Sloan cited a risk that Treasury prices could go lower "on the back of the dollar today."
But he added that the market could be fairly quiet until Thursday's retail sales report.
"Retail sales and PPI (Producer Price Index) and initial (jobless) claims should be quite important," said Sloan.

Sloan said he is forecasting "quite a sharp reversal" in weekly initial unemployment claims to 315,000 from last week's surge to 337,000. Economists polled by Reuters forecasted, on average, 326,000 new claims for the week ended June 7.

The government will release its report on May retail sales on Thursday. Economists look for a 0.4 percent sales increase, reversing April's 0.3 percent decline. Excluding autos, retail sales are being forecast at up 0.3 percent in May after a decline of 0.1 percent in April.

The May Producer Price Index, set for release on Friday, is expected to be up 0.1 percent after a 0.6 percent drop in April. The core PPI, the index without its more volatile food and energy components, is also expected to be up 0.1 percent following a 0.1 percent decline in April.

"We really don't get much of anything in the way of economic data until Thursday," said Lee Youngdahl, bond market analyst at Aubrey G. Lanston. "There's very little to point to this morning. There's a little bit of a markdown going on. It got pretty frothy on Friday. Maybe the attitude is more sober today, but it's certainly not taking back the entire gain."
The Treasury will sell $14.0 billion in three- and six-month bills at 1300 EDT/1700 GMT.
"The bill auctions are on the small side these days and that tends to buttress the rising price argument," Youndahl said.

As for the role of the dollar in the Treasury market's performance, Youngdahl said the weaker dollar could take some of the speculative fervor out of the strong dollar play that was "allegedly very strong" on Friday. But Youngdahl said the U.S. unit is assumed to retain fundamental strength against the mark and other European currencies.
Three- and six-month bill rates were unchanged at 4.92 percent and 5.17 percent, respectively. Year bill rates were up one basis point to 5.39 percent.

Two-year notes were down 1/32 to 100-8/32, yielding 6.11 percent. Five-year notes were priced at 100-14/32, down 3/32 to yield 6.40 percent. Ten-year notes were trading at 100-26/32, down 5/32, to yield 6.51 percent.
